In addressing the trends outlined above, the literature on critical security studies (CSS) contains particularly helpful insights into how security logics function politically as they reach into and engulf new corners of contemporary society, such as the realm of nutrition. Broadly speaking, critical studies on security are taken up by scholars who question the state-centric and positivist assumptions of traditional security studies – such as the role of predictable, causal mechanisms in shaping inter-state conflict in an anarchic world order – particularly as the debates about and practices of security have changed so dramatically since the end of the Cold War (Collective 2006). These discussions began with the Copenhagen School, where theorists analysed the impacts of securitising topic-areas beyond those that were explicitly militaristic, including the political, societal, environmental, and economic (Buzan, Waever, and de Wilde 1998). The concern was that naming something a security issue functions as a spoken act wherein elite actors can convince relevant audiences to accept exceptional measures to safeguard a referent object in the face of a whatever constitutes an extensional threat, all the while circumventing ‘normal’ governmental processes.

CSS has since expanded to include other approaches that examine how securitisation operates in diffuse and distinct ways depending on the context (Browning and McDonald 2013). Those who employ sociological perspectives, for example, expose security professionals, everyday surveillance systems, and political–economic relations as key mediators of security (Balzacq 2019; Bigo 2017). At the same time, scholars focusing on emancipatory interpretations of food security emphasise the need to widen the scope of agency over food systems through working with and supporting local and regional movements that challenge the structural sources of hunger (Barthwal-Datta and Basu 2017; Shepard 2012). As Richardson and Nunes (2015, 7) argue, ‘in some circumstances security can be seen as an emancipatory means for dealing with food problems – in other words, food-as-security may enable a transformation in political procedure that broadens the capacity of those involved to influence the course of their lives.’

The important questions, overall, are then: does the instrument of securitisation serve to challenge or reinforce underlying conditions that perpetuate food precarity, counter or expand the technical and managerial resolutions, or empower or exploit communities? While researchers are indeed raising such questions about food security (as detailed above), this critical orientation has yet to be sufficiently applied to the distinct ways in which nutrition has become the subject of intensified global security debates. We contend that leveraging insights from critical security studies serves as an apt starting point through which to call on scholars and practitioners to engage in more theoretically rigorous work that can both expose and subvert the prevailing political discourse on nutritional crisis. CSS specifically draws our attention towards 1) the implications of discourse for legitimacy and the formations of subjectivity 2) the structural barriers to and drivers of insecurity, and 3) the role of alternative, emancipatory approaches. In the following section, we use these key insights to introduce a critical lens through which to grapple with nutritional crises.

Thus, we organise this framework into three relevant components: discourse, structure, and resistance.

In this context, it is unsurprising that the majority of the ‘at-risk’ populations discussed by groups like the Global Network Against Food Crisis are situated within the global South, where ‘women and children living in food-crisis countries are especially vulnerable to malnutrition’ and ‘in total 7.2 million children suffered from wasting in the 10 worst food crises and 31.9 million suffered from stunting’ (FSIN and Global Network Against Food Crises 2021, 18).

Who is the ‘healthy’ subject, and against whom are they positioned? What constitutes ‘good’ nutrition, and how does discursively securitising nutrition reinforce the uneven power dynamics that inform universalised notions of ‘good’ in this context? What are the effects of repeatedly classifying populations as wasted, stunted, deficient, and in-crisis while attempting to govern an ‘alarming nutrition situation’ (FSIN and Global Network Against Food Crises 2023, 45–46)? In sum, we argue that scholars should explicitly draw from critical security studies literature to develop an understanding of the performativity of the discourses in which concerns about ‘food and nutritional security’ are embedded. Assessing the performativity of security in relation to nutrition entails questioning how security classifies certain groups as threatening, risky, or vulnerable, whether emergency rhetoric side-lines democratic deliberation about food systems, in what ways securitisation takes on state-centric or globalised dimensions, and whether securitisation can serve justice-oriented objectives (Bigo 2017; Booth 2007; Buzan, Waever, and de Wilde 1998). More broadly, a critical perspective should remain attuned to the ways the meaning of ‘crisis’ in relation to food and specifically nutrition is constructed contested, and re-articulated by different groups.

Second, we encourage an attentiveness to the capitalist and neoliberal structures that shape the modes of discourse and decision-making through which the politics of nutrition and securitisation intersect.
